items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: He was also a very agreable fellow and we began to be good friends although I did not speak French and he didn't speak English.

ctx.x: in Boston. "Chit" was fast as [and] lightning and he must have heard Art Tatum many times and studied his style. He was the next thing to Art as far as technique was concerned. But he never wanted to bass to accompany him on his solos. He had a good left hand and I suppose he had the idea that the bass did not play the same pattern as he did with his left hand and it disturbed his ideas.

D'Hellemes was a good solid bass player who preferred to play trombone. He was also a very agreable fellow and we began to be good friends although I did not speak French and he didn't speak English. The first date with Chit and Eugene was recorded for Ultraphone. We recorded again the 31st of January '36 for His Master's Voice and did "I'm in the Mood for Love" and "After You've Gone". Those two records added more to my European success than the Fats Waller ones in the sense that I had more solo space and I was…

A little earlier than the January 31st date with Chittison and d'Hellemes, I recorded "Coquette" and the first number I ever composed called "Joe Louis Stomp" with Edgar Courance (tenor), John Ferrier (piano), Oscar Aleman (guitar), Eugene d'Hellemes (bass), and William Diemar (drums). This date is registered in the French discography as being done on the 31st of January also but I don't remember having two recording dates the same day.
